subject: Banking
title: The Microsoft-Activision Saga
description: A quick win: understand The Microsoft-Activision Saga.

hook.text: Microsoft paid $69 billion for Activision Blizzard in 2023. It was the largest gaming acquisition in history.

buildup.text: The deal gave Microsoft Call of Duty, World of Warcraft, and Candy Crush.

discovery.text: UK, EU, and US regulators challenged the deal. Concerns centered on Microsoft gaining too much power in cloud gaming.

twist.text: Microsoft offered concessions including licensing Call of Duty to rivals for 10 years.

climax.text: The Activision deal showed that mega-mergers now require global regulatory approval.

punchline.text: $69 billion, 21 months, three continents of regulators. Welcome to mega-deals.

quiz.question: What concession helped Microsoft close the Activision deal?
options: Licensing Call of Duty to rival platforms for 10 years

details.summary: Microsoft's 68.7 billion dollar acquisition of Activision Blizzard in 2023 was the largest gaming deal in history, requiring over a year of antitrust battles across multiple jurisdictions before finally receiving regulatory approval.
details.whyItMatters: The Microsoft-Activision deal tested the limits of modern antitrust enforcement in tech. It showed that regulators increasingly scrutinize large tech acquisitions, even when the buyer and target are not direct competitors.
takeaways: Microsoft paid 68.7 billion for Activision Blizzard in 2023
The FTC, EU, and UK CMA all investigated the deal
Microsoft made concessions on game exclusivity to win approval

faq.question: Why did regulators try to block this acquisition?
faq.answer: Concerns centered on Microsoft potentially making popular Activision games like Call of Duty exclusive to Xbox, harming PlayStation competition. Cloud gaming market concentration and Microsoft's growing power in gaming also worried regulators.

faq.question: What concessions did Microsoft make?
faq.answer: Microsoft agreed to 10-year licensing deals ensuring Call of Duty would remain on PlayStation and Nintendo. It also offered cloud gaming rights to competitors. These commitments addressed the specific competition concerns regulators raised.
